utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T. The Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we discussed with the Defence last night -- we discussed with the Defence last night the timetabling of matters before the Chamber, and we are agreed that a different order could be usefully employed from that forecast yesterday for the following reasons: First, it's really important, if not vital, that we have a decision on the transcript witnesses at the earliest possible moment. Because if any other witnesses have to be called, we must be putting steps in hand to get them here as quickly as possible, particularly if there is any prospect of using any part of next week. Secondly, there is a witness who is a witness from Bosnia, who is a woman, not in her first flush of youth, and I think it's thought desirable, if we can, to have her evidence taken ahead of Dr. Ribicic's evidence. And I gather there is no objection to that general rescheduling of matters, subject to the Chamber's approval. Dr. Ribicic would not, of course, then be finished today, but that doesn't present a difficulty for him. So, with your leave, maybe do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: We have no problems with that. We did ask the Prosecution, if they were going to change the order, to send us the summaries by 8.00 last night. As to the woman who was about to testify, that summary arrived at our office at 10.30 in the evening, after, mercifully, we were gone. And to be of much use to us, we would like to have it well in advance. Similarly, Dr. Ribicic's summary was given to us this morning. There were corrections made to it. Again, to be at all helpful, we need them well in advance. I would like to raise, if I may, two other issues. First, yesterday I mentioned the Prosecution's inconsistent position on Mr. Elford's resume. I would like to know from the Prosecution if they are going to give us his resume.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you slow down, Mr. Stein, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think there has been any inconsistency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's not deal with this in a confrontational way. Who is Mr. Elford?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Elford is the person who -- let me start at the beginning. I have explained in court that calling someone an expert is not going to elevate him into that position. I've explained in court what I know about his background. And apparently that isn't sufficient for the Defence. He's a witness who has produced a map, at the request of the Court. He's what's called a military analyst here. He served some time in the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can be cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He can be cross-examined on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: With respect, sir, all you need to do is read the report, and you will, and you'll see it's beyond just a map. It's an analysis of a variety --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we -- it seems to me to be far exceeding what is needed. We'll set it down for argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good, sir. Would you also, if it please the Court, the Prosecution has used in its exhibits and a variety of requests a series of ECMM reports. They have used them with various witnesses. In this case they certainly do have a library, because they were all requested from the ECMM, and given subject to Rule 70. I tried to negotiate something with Mr. Nice. We've been unable to do so. And this is one of those instances where I think the doctrine of completeness requires that all the ECMM documents in the Prosecution's possession be turned over to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was matter I was going to raise ex parte. There is no such thing as a doctrine of completeness. This is a subtle way of the Defence trying to get round the Rule for mutual disclosure. They have avoided providing any documents themselves. We provided every ECMM document that we are obliged to provide by production of a witness or under Rule 68. And we are constrained by Rule 70 in relation to the balance. But I want to raise this matter, in any event, as one of a number of matters to be raised ex parte.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we'll do that. Yes, are there any other matters to be dealt with now, before we have the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, we were going to deal, if we could, in advance, with the question of the transcripts for the reasons that I advanced. We need to know if any of these witnesses has to be called in order to put matters in hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I am not in a position to deal with that today. I need thoroughly to read the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Can I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, with regard to the transcript, we cannot -- of course we cannot discuss the transcripts now. But there is one thing, though, which came as a surprise to you, and that is that we have before us such enormous quantity of pages. I believe it was the figure of 6.000 pages was mentioned. And I am not asking you to answer me now, but I believe you should think about a method which could be as follows: You should select from this transcript those paragraphs which have most direct bearing on the case which is before us, that is the Kordic/Cerkez case. And even if you are producing the whole transcript, again we have to deal only with those parts which have a direct bearing on this case. That would mean more practical access for the Defence to this transcript, and it would also help them to deal with it, in view of this huge mass of documents which were shown to us yesterday. I should like you to think about a method which would allow you to produce them, while avoiding at the same time the difficulties which have to do with the huge and impressive mass of this transcript. And also one should bear in mind that the decision in the Aleksovski case should not be used beyond certain particular circumstances. What it means is that all the transcripts cannot be produced or taken from one case to the other without particular justification. The case, Aleksovski, has to do with some particular circumstances and the decision was taken in this regard. And those were exceptional and particular circumstances. And in view of all of that, I believe you should reconsider your application to produce the transcripts from one case to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just to respond briefly to that. The transcripts, as a method of abbreviating the time that live evidence would take, is something strongly advocated by the Chamber at earlier stages, and we have been responsive to that. Secondly, the possibility of using only extracts from the transcripts is, indeed, an appealing one and one with which we are entirely content. Indeed, I had always envisaged, and still envisage, the transcripts admitted will be, as it were, admitted without there being necessarily any duty on the Judges to read the transcript slavishly, or necessarily at all, until referred to passages of the evidence in the argument of the parties. We know, of course, that the Judges have available to them staff who can further assist them in the preparation of material. So we're entirely happy with that as a general method of process and would look forward to relying on the transcripts as and when necessary in the course of our closing or other arguments. The only fly in that particular ointment is that the Defence, particularly in relation to Blaskic, say that it isn't appropriate to take the transcripts in part and they have to be taken in whole. With that view, we don't necessarily agree, but that's a problem standing in the way of the course that Your Honour recommends. As to the observation that there is, in some way, the need to reconsider in general the quantity of material we are putting in or seeking to put in by transcript, we reject that, save for a few witnesses who Mr. Scott and Mr. Lopez-Terres have been able to consider can perhaps now be removed from the list, but otherwise we reject that proposition. I was going to say at some stage, and I'll make the point now, there is at the moment, it appears, an inclination in the Tribunal to exclude evidence and to hold us responsible for the time the trial has taken, but in due course, I must ensure that the Tribunal recognises --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Mr. Nice, I thought I would say what I had to say and then we would have to move to the witness, not to launch a discussion. You said that you wanted to see whether you can present to us these extracts. Please, how is there a way in which we can present them as a whole? Think about it, and then when the time comes, we shall have a lengthy discussion about that. I do not really want to go into a debate now. If you can think about a method in order to improve on the production of transcripts, then you will tell us and we shall be discussing, when the time comes, how to do all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then to conclude at this stage until the matter is more fully argued, the position is we've had a response in schedule form from the Defence which we've considered. To go through in court each one of those objections would take a great deal of the Court's time. It seems to us that the objections are capable of being dealt -- sorry. The objections are frequently generic, they can be dealt with generically. What I would respectfully invite of the Chamber is this: If it could find the time to consider that schedule as a priority, we could address our observations generically to it, and it might then be possible for the matter to be ruled with attention to particular witnesses as required. We will also, Mr. Scott, Mr. Lopez-Terres, or I, be in a position to indicate which witnesses we take the view we can dispense with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The sooner we have that, the better because it will save a great deal of time for everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Scott -- I can give you the numbers or Mr. Scott can give you the numbers straightaway, of the ones we are contingently -- we are prepared to dispense with. Don't give the chart out now. Using the original numbers, it's numbers 9, 13, 14, and 42.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the Chamber could do that, we'd be very grateful because it will assist us. I don't believe this is too early, but may I seek a short ex parte hearing. It's to deal with, I think, about four topics, one of which was going to be ECMM, and there are a couple of witnesses whose attendance is the subject of methods of compulsion, and we typically do deal with those ex parte, although I know it's an inconvenience to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll find a convenient time either today or tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me deal with something while we're dealing with administrative matters, and that's two dates: Next Wednesday, the 23rd, will be a Chambers afternoon. We shall not be sitting. I think that was already scheduled in advance. We have been considering the position between the two cases, and in particular dealing with any motion of no-case or judgement of acquittal. We've come to the conclusion that an oral hearing on that may be necessary for clarification of the submissions, and we will schedule that for Thursday, the 30th of March, at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Scott is going to be taking the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We haven't got the summaries. We've got the application but not the summaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a motion for protective measures that should be dealt with, obviously, in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Before the witness is sworn, may I just bring to the Court's attention two -- three items, actually. Two are my fault, as eyes are failing. In the outline or the summary provided, on page 2, in paragraph 6, the sentence which starts "The Constitutional Court of BiH" should read "in invalidating..." It is an important change and it is my fault again; in proofing, I missed it. So it should read, "The Constitutional Court of BiH in invalidating ..." It is on page 2, it is point number 6. Then one other thing that my eyes missed. On page 11, point number 57, it should read: "President of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna ..." The parentheses indicate it is HZ HB, but this should be clearer for the Court and for counsel, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is one person whose attendance should be mentioned on the record. Ms. Andrea Matacic of the Office of the Prosecutor has assisted in this preparation of this matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, would you state your full name, date of birth, and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: My name is Ciril Ribicic. I was born in Ljubljana on the 30th of June, 1947.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And by nationality, you are?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: By nationality, I am a Slovene and citizen of the Republic of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you indicate your educational degrees, please.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the faculty of law. My M.A. and Ph.D. was conducted at the faculty of law in Ljubljana.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Currently what is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: I am at the same time a member of the Slovenia parliament and full professor of constitutional law at the faculty of law in Ljubljana.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What is your political party affiliation and what was it in 1990?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: I belonged to the League of Communists of Slovenia which was a component part up until 1990 of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. I now belong to the Associated List of Social Democrats of Slovenia which is a member of the Socialist International.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'd ask, please, that the audio personnel show the video, which is Z2683.1. Prior to the commencement, so the Court knows, it is from the BBC's "The Death of Yugoslavia". They are relevant clips pertaining to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we've never seen this before. I wonder if we might have a transcript so that we can follow what's being said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I doubt you can. Yes, let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: For His Honour Judge Bennouna, this clip is available in French as well. We will provide it and transcripts will be provided as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, after you left the 14th party congress in Belgrade, what did you, as a member of the party, or if you were president of the party, what did you do then on behalf of Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Let me first say that this tape is important because you can see that everything did not begin in Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Dr. Ribicic. Could you tell us the exact date of the scene that we have just witnessed on videotape for the present?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes. We left Belgrade on the 22nd of January, 1990, at 22.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, you were asked by counsel, after you left the party congress, what you did then on behalf of Slovenia. You were going to reply something to the effect of the tape being important. Could you bear in mind, please, that we have your statement, we also have a summary of it. Time is not unlimited and counsel knows what the matters are which are relevant, so we would be grateful if you would concentrate, please, on just answering the questions which she asks. Yes, would you ask that again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, following the departure of the Slovene delegation from Belgrade, as is evidenced here, what did you, in your role as, I believe, president of the party at the time, do on behalf of Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: After my departure from Belgrade, when it was clear that Yugoslavia would no longer exist, in Slovenia, we'd organised ourselves to prepare a plebiscite. In my conviction, the most important act was the signing of an agreement on the part of all the parliamentary political parties with regard to a plebiscite, at which the citizens of Slovenia would decide on their independence and the Republic's independence. On behalf of my party, I signed that agreement. Later on, I took part in the elaboration of a new constitution of the Republic of Slovenia, which was adopted after the Republic's independence in November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, the part that you took, did it involve the actual drafting of the documents? Were you involved at that level?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was President of a task force which was entrusted with drafting the part of the constitution relating to the government in the Republic of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you, in your current role as both a member of parliament and as a professor of law, retain contacts and favourable relations with persons, including governmental persons, in Croatia, the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I know most of the members of the new Croatian government well, and I have maintained contacts with some other representatives as well of the government and authorities in Croatia up to the present.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: One of those persons, was that the Ivica Racan who was depicted in the film we just saw, who is now Prime Minister of Yugoslavia? I'm sorry, of Croatia, excuse me. Strike that.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I met Mr. Ivica Racan many times in our capacity as party presidents, because both of us led parties which today are members of the Socialist International.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, turning to your report. If you are handed now -- if the usher would be kind enough to hand a copy of a document which has already been tendered into evidence. It is Z27.2, which is the founding document of Herceg-Bosna, as well as handing you the volume which is essentially Volume 1 of Narodni List. I'll ask you several questions. We will not be long. But I'll ask you several questions about your report. Your Honours, the Office of the Prosecutor has provided a complete bound set of the Narodni List to the Registry for the use of the Court. The Defence has been provided with these documents, and they are just for your own deliberations and use. Just so you that know, some are translated, some are not, but the Court may wish to have them throughout the pendency of the case. Those are untranslated. The documents that Dr. Ribicic will take a glance at is a pile of documents from the first volume, which Ms. Bauer can distribute, in English and in French as well. And also the decision on Herceg-Bosna is in English and French as well, although the Court has seen it. Dr. Ribicic, looking at what is marked Z27.2, which you have in the Croatian language. This document is from the 18th of November, 1991, and it is the foundational document on the creation of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. This document, as well as the many provisions that are contained in Volume 1 of Narodni List, all of which we do not need to address today. But can you indicate, did these serve as part of the basis of the analysis as to the nature of the polity referred to as either HZ HB or HR-HB?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I started my analysis on the establishment and functioning of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna by reading those very documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, can you comment, once you began the analysis, where would you start from in looking at the nature of the polity of Herceg-Bosna? What considerations would you assess?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: When I saw this extensive material, I asked myself which would be the theoretical basis for judging what had taken place on the territory of Herceg-Bosna. And I looked into textbooks and other books related to the theory of statehood, and I concentrated my efforts on the issue and elements, the minimum elements which must be fulfilled, met, in order for us to be able to speak about a state proper. And I found that there were three classical elements, and that all, practically all professors teaching the theory of states, states in the world, and especially the theoreticians who worked or are still working today at the different faculties of law on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, that is to say in Croatia, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Slovenia, in Macedonia, that they all looked at those elements. The fourth element was the immediate sub -- into international law, and I took this from the book by Dr. Pitamic, who was one of the founders of the faculty of law in Ljublijana at which I work.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, the three classical provisions of, as it were, emerging states, could you describe them? And then we can discuss Dr. Pitamic's provision about subordination to international law.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: As I said, there are three basic elements inherent in every state, and that is territory, population, and a sovereign government, or effective government.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you say "effective government," do you mean a government which is carrying out its own policies as opposed to the policies of another sovereign, which may be superior to it?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: It is quite clear that we cannot speak about a sovereign government, or effective government in cases where it is not effective on its territory, and especially if it is subordinated to some other state, or if it is attempting to be successful on a territory where some other authority is sovereign or effective.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Could you, very briefly, discuss the subordination to international law that Dr. Pitamic referred to?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Leonid Pitamic in his book entitled "The State" emphasises that sovereignty exists and that the sovereign of states has become a relatively element in each given state, because every sovereign state should be subordinated to international law. And this position is an interesting one, because it was published in his book in the 1920s. What is particularly emphasised by Dr. Pitamic, and which was significant for my own analysis of Herceg-Bosna, was the fact that he speaks about immediate subordination to international law. That is to say that we cannot speak about an independent and sovereign state unless it were immediately subordinated to international law.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Dr. Ribicic. When you say "immediately," do you mean directly?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: I used the word direct subordination, immediate subordination to international law.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Would this type of analysis also be the type of analysis used in, for example, creating or looking at the constitution of Slovenia, or Croatia, or any other country?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes, this theoretical foundation would be interesting in analysing the inception of every new state, and especially the states that emerged in -- from the 1970s onwards in the last ten years.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Having looked to see if these elements were present in the enactments, that is in the official written pronouncements that came from Herceg-Bosna, did you find that all the elements were formally, at least on paper, present in both HZ HB and/or HR-HB?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. That is to say, in the documents which were published in the Narodni List, Official Gazette, as the Official Gazette of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, all those four elements are listed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, when you undertake a constitutional analysis, do you only, as a professor or as an expert generally on statehood, do you generally deal only with the de jure or on paper written enactments, or do you consider other factors in your analysis?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: It is quite clear that modern, legal theory stems from normative acts, but it also must bear in mind their implementation in practice, and how they are realised in practice. And this is especially true for a constitutional legal analysis, which cannot only stop at an analysis of legal acts and enactments, but must study how they are put into practice. And therefore it differentiates, on the one hand, between the constitution, as it has been envisaged and normativated from the constitution that has been translated into practical daily life.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Somers, if I have understood correctly, you have asked questions concerning the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, its characteristics in order to learn whether it corresponds to the criteria of statehood, that is to say the existence of a territory population and effective government controlling that territory, and that population, and its subordination and its respect to international laws directly, and linked to international law generally. I should like to ask Dr. Ribicic now whether, with respect to that last element, and to the whole, what the links were between the communities of Herceg-Bosna and the state of Croatia? Was this link of direct subordination to international law also realised there? All the more so because it was not recognised by the states and, on the other hand, whether the power, if it existed, this power existed in Herceg-Bosna, and the community of Herceg-Bosna, was it totally autonomous with respect to the state of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, would you care for Dr. Ribicic directly to answer those or to be answered in the course of my additional questions? But if you'd like to have it developed this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like him to answer directly, if he would. Dr. Ribicic.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as the enactments are concerned themselves, that is to say, the contents of the Official Gazette as a document of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, it would appear that all these elements, including the fourth element, were realised, implemented. But if we take into account the different testimony of the participants, and I should particularly like to stress the testimonies that were important for me and that was those by participants from the HDZ, for example, and most particularly Mr. Stipe Mesic and Mr. Klujic, and if we take into consideration the documents which I was able to read through which testified to political meetings between the leadership of the HDZ of Croatia and the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina, then we get a completely different picture of the situation in general in Herceg-Bosna, and this is particularly true with respect to the fourth element. From those testimonies and from that material, it would appear, that is to say, two things emerge: First, that in many respects the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was de facto subordinated to the organs and bodies of the neighbouring state, that is to say, the Republic of Croatia; second, that in certain cases, even intentionally, normative acts were used to mask that existing and actual state of affairs. I would like to refer in this connection to a discussion between Mr. Juric at a meeting in Zagreb, held in Zagreb, where the top representatives of the HDZ of Croatia and the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina met, and I quote them in note number 2, and it reads: "At the level of diplomacy, our political personages in Sarajevo can continue to pledge that they are in favour of a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina." Something similar was stated before this Tribunal by Witness Stjepan Kljuic, and I quote an article in Slobodna Bosna when he said the following, and I quote: "The plan was formally to advocate a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina, while in reality doing quite the opposite, in other words, they worked against it because they did not want it." From these brief quotations, it emerges that part of the normative acts of Herceg-Bosna were devised to mask the real relationship that existed with the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Court, the references to the meeting are already in evidence under Z2717, which was the transcript of minutes of a meeting that was introduced through Dr. Kljuic, and there are a number of passages that are clearly available in the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, are you then saying that there were two levels on which an analysis had to be conducted? Is it a two-track or two-tier approach?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I noted down in my opinion that we were, in fact, dealing with two stories, two different stories, Bosnia and Herzegovina. One is the one emerging from the normative acts and which demonstrates the intention to form a new independent autonomous state community, whereas the other stems from the testimonies and different documents in existence which speak of a high level of dependency of the Bosnia-Herzegovinian organs and bodies -- I apologise, the organs of Herceg-Bosna on the neighbouring Republic of Croatia. Perhaps the best example of this would be to look at a quotation from the meeting that I mentioned, on the 27th of December, 1991, that took place in Zagreb, where President Tudjman, who was the chairman of the meeting, spoke about issues such as customs, tariffs, petrol, money matters, and borders, and we can see that his positions were later on, so to speak, translated; that is to say, they became the basis for the adoption of the types of acts that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna enacted. Therefore, if we were to base our analysis exclusively on the enactments passed, it would appear that we were dealing with a state community which was fully independent and autonomous of Croatia. Let me add that as far as relationships with Bosnia-Herzegovina go, this difference between the two approaches is not so marked, so much in evidence. So as far as the relationship towards Bosnia-Herzegovina goes, both in normative terms and in de facto terms, Herceg-Bosna was becoming independent of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, of the meeting to which you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The meeting to which you refer, at that meeting, just to refresh our memories, what types of persons were present at that meeting with Dr. Tudjman in his office on the 27th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: According to the record, those were the highest dignitaries of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Bosnia-Herzegovina, both those who worked in Sarajevo and those who worked in the Herceg-Bosna territory; on the other hand, the highest standing officials of the Croat Democratic Community of the Republic of Croatia, who at that time were also discharging the top-most state functions, duties, in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In other words, it was an HDZ meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: It was an HDZ meeting, but at the same time the HDZ officials were at that time discharging the most important duties, especially in Croatia, but also in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Herceg-Bosna, so that that was a meeting of officials from those two republics; naturally, those who belonged to the Croat Democratic Community.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were Dario Kordic and Mate Boban present at that meeting and participants in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were active participants in that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In order to give the benefit of having in front of them some of the documents that were referred to, we have translations as well as originals of some of those provisions. They'd be Z341.6, Z341.7, and I think there's a third one, Z341.9. They were some of the provisions of customs, of the various types of concerns that were raised in establishing the enactments of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, do you have any opinion on the basis of the choice of municipalities included in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Herceg-Bosna embraced 30 municipalities. When I looked at those municipalities and then saw the advice of experts who know about this more than I do, I established that all those municipalities had different ethnic compositions, and only some of those 30 municipalities did the Croats represent a majority ethnic group. In others, Croats had the relative majority, and in others again were a minority. At the time, when a decision was taken to set up the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, they did not have the majority in a number of those municipalities. So I asked people who knew more about this what might be the reason for the inclusion of those 30 municipalities, and most of the answers that I received were that this was the territory which had made an integral part of the Banovina of Croatia of 1939; that is, that this was the territory which the Croats believed had been unfairly lost as a result of World War II. In other words, this was an attempt to restore the Croat state within the boundaries that the Banovina of Croatia had. Naturally, it could not be achieved only by attaching the 30 municipalities, but also with the attachment of some other territories. Dr. Franjo Tudjman never stopped insisting on the importance of the fact that the Banovina of Croatia was mentioned in the preamble to the Croatian constitution which is now in effect, and that is what was also mentioned at the meeting that I already mentioned, held on the 27th of December, 1991. In his statement for Oslobodenje, Mate Boban related Herceg-Bosna to -- and I'm quoting, "in putting the banovina," I am quoting, "within the boundaries which the Croat people had at the outset of World War II." Dr. Zdravko Tomac speaks about this in his latest book, "Crime Without Punishment." It is in chapter 27 and it says, "Tomac believes," I'm quoting, "that within the boundaries of the former Banovina of Croatia, on the eve of World War II, that Croatia's territory has been increased by Istru, Zadar, the islands, and Medzimurje, and that that particular territory was Tudjman's ideal." I think that these are the reasons why those 30 municipalities were singled out, and also in the documents of Herceg-Bosna, we read about the historical lands and defence of Croat ethnic and historical lands. So the formulation about historical lands also seems to direct us, to point in the direction of the Banovina of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you aware of any comments by the late President Tudjman about the need for this territory for the defence of Croatia, in terms of its physical shape and its concerns with neighbouring potential aggression?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Late Dr. Tudjman referred to -- addressed this issue at that meeting, on the 27th of December '91, saying that in the light of Croatia's interests, it was important for Bosnia-Herzegovina to join Croatia. And I shall quote his view. He says that, "In the light of the Croat identity, the territory and the organisation of the state in every respect possible." So my answer is in the affirmative, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask the usher --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask the usher, please, to present Z342.2; the document with a translation in English at this time affixed. I hope we'll be able to get a French one in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, this document, which is essentially a balance sheet or a financial document that was taken from the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Ministry of Defence office in Mostar, makes reference on one of the first pages, where you see figures, it says a structure -- the financial support of the structure support from 1/1/93 to 31/12/93. That is the page. If you could look down the page, the second half of the page where it says the amounts received in Deutschemarks DM. Do you see a figure that refers to monies coming from the Ministry of Defence of Republic of Croatia in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And could you give the amount, please, for that figure that came from the Republic of Croatia, Ministry of Defence to the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: 19.206 million German marks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I was looking, I think, at the 268.770. We are looking at a different place, perhaps. You are looking at the total. I am looking at the top figure where it says, "Ministry of Defence of Republic of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I see. 268.770.000 German marks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, turning now to the actual position and functions of the presidency in Herceg-Bosna. Looking first at the original decision on the establishment of HZ HB, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, back in 1991. Can you please discuss some of your observations and conclusions about the position and the functions of the presidency, and what it is? It would help, I believe, to distribute Z341.2, which I believe has previously -- I'm sorry, it has not previously. It is translated. It is the Rules of Procedure of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: If one looks at the original decision on the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, that is not the one of September, '92, which was published in Narodni List in September, 1992, but the decision taken at the meeting, when it was decided to establish a Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And there one notes major discrepancies as regards to the presidency. Then also the original decision -- also it comes from this original decision, that a presidency is the only and the supreme authority, body of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Now, the wording which refers to the top leadership of the community is in this regard of particular import in the textbook on "The Theory of States" by Vjekoslav Milicic, present professor of "The Theory of States" at the faculty of law in Zagreb. It is pointed out that in the Croatian language, and in the Croatian theory of state, the term Vrhonistvo, the top leadership, means the sovereignty of the state authority. That is, it means the supreme, the top sovereign power. And from that point of view it is, therefore, quite clear that, according to the original decision, the presidency was conceived not only as the top most, but also as the only authority, body of the newly emerged polity. Secondly, another thing which is considerably at odds with the subsequent polity decision, relates to the officials of that presidency. According to the original decision, the presidency elects the president, two vice-presidents and a secretary. That is, according to the original decision, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna does not have the president of the Croatian Community, and all they have are the officials of the presidency, that is four members: The president, two vice-presidents, and the secretary.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, just to clarify. Can you describe what is the presidency? Because you drew a distinction between a president and the presidency. Can you elaborate a bit more, please?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: The role of the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna appears only the decision on the establishment published in September, '92. That is, the original decision makes no mention of this. In the early months of the community of Herceg-Bosna, it did not have a president, a president who could be called a head of state or the highest authority or anything like it. It had presidency consisting of four members, the most important of them, surely, being the president, followed by his two vice-presidents and the secretary. In some of the conclusions which were adopted by the presidency subsequently, these officials were empowered with representing the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in different types of negotiations, talks and political meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And where was the source of that empowerment? Was it in the actual normative enactment, or where does one observe the source of that empowerment?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: The decision itself, stipulating that the presidency was the top-most leadership of the community, determined which one was the most important or, rather, the only authority in that community. As for some special powers, we could read about that in the record which I already mentioned repeatedly, and which address a meeting of the presidency expanded, held on the 23rd of December that year in Tomislavgrad. The secretary of the presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna read out the conclusions of that meeting four days later in Zagreb. And I can quote the conclusion listed in that record, which addresses the officials in the presidency. So this was the fourth conclusion of the meeting held in Tomislavgrad. I am quoting: "The President, Mr. Mate Boban; vice-president's, Bozo Rajic and Dario Kordic; and the secretary, Ignac Kostroman, are vested with full authority to represent the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna at a meeting in Zagreb, on the 27th of December, '91, and in records and in the future with regard to the future programme activities of Herceg-Bosna, and the Croat Democratic Union of Herceg-Bosna." Even without that special decision, it would have been quite clear that all the crucial functions at the time between the meetings, at the times when the presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna did not sit, that in the interim periods all the duties were discharged by the members of the presidency, that is the president, two vice-presidents and the secretary.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, the four names which you just enumerated: Boban, Kordic, Rajic, Bozo Rajic, and Kostroman. Are those the four individuals who comprised the presidency of Herceg-Bosna, to which you have been referring?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: No, the presidency had more members. The presidency also comprised presidents from 13 municipalities, that is municipalities comprising the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Article 7 of the original decision on the establishment on the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, it says that the top-most leadership of the community is the presidency, consisting of representatives of the Croat people in municipal authorities; that all presidents of the municipal boards of the Croat Democratic Union. And paragraph 2 of the same article says that the presidency elects the president, two vice-presidents and the secretary. In other words, the presidency had more members, but these were the four functions which was singled out, which were specified.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Those four individuals whose names I read, along with the other members of the presidency, comprise the entire presidency, as I understand it. Dr. Ribicic, you mentioned --

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: -- that only the Croat people -- are you able to comment on whether or not there was any inclusion of other nationalities, or was the HZ HB a mono-national, mono-party institution?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: If we look at the reasoned opinion underpinning this original decision, we can see that the idea was that there should be a community --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt. Where is the witness reading from, please? It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, these --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, these points are from a combination of the statutes, the enactments of Herceg-Bosna, as well as the minutes on the stenogram of the meeting of 27 December. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: What I have just quoted is from the recent opinion of the original decision on the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Which is Z27.2, which the Court was given earlier. Dr. Ribicic, are you aware of any empowerment that was given by the Croatian Community, or by Herceg-Bosna to President Franjo Tudjman with respect to representing its interests?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the meeting that I already mentioned, the 23rd of December '91 in Tomislavgrad, one of the conclusions addressed that matter, that is it was concluded there that the president of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, could represent the interests of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You have indicated -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: May I quote the conclusion? It comes from the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Unless it's -- counsel wants you to, I think we've got the point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If the Court would have no objection, it should be highlighted. I believe it would be very beneficial to hear it. It's brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Very quickly, Dr. Ribicic, please.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: It reads as follows: "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna fully authorises Dr. Franjo Tudjman as the president of the Republic of Croatia and the president of the Croat Democratic Union to represent the interests of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna with the international factors, and in inter-party and inter-republic negotiations about the definition of the definitive boundaries of the Republic of Croatia." That was this authorisation given, the powers given to the president of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: An additional question about the presidency and the role of the vice-president of the presidency. Does it appear, from what you have just told the Court, that there was any limitation on whether or not the vice-president could act only in a legislative capacity, or could the vice-president act in executive, administrative or other capacity necessary to the sovereignty or the sovereign running of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: For the first time the acts of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna says that the presidency representative body, but it is mentioned for the first time in the amendments of the 3rd of July, '92, and published in September, '92. In the original decision it reads that the presidency is the top-most leadership of the community. So we could say that this is a body which discharges both representative functions, that is the functions of the parliament, and the head of a state, and the government. From that point of view, the -- there are no limitations, as far as the vice-presidents are concerned, that they must only be vice-presidents of the presidency as a representative body.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. However, at that initial period, they, in effect, were the government? That is correct? I'm sorry, I didn't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. Even though I do not have any documents which would relate to that early period to know anything more about how things looked like in practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you able to address the position of Herceg-Bosna in either its community or republic form, with its relationship toward the organs and authority of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Was there any pronouncement by Bosnia that indicates the overall relationship of Herceg-Bosna to it, and it to Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Briefly speaking, in the documents and Acts adopted by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, at the beginning it was the presidency, and later on the HVO, Bosnia-Herzegovina in formal terms was present. That meant that the name "Bosnia-Herzegovina" was to be found on the heading on page 1 of the Official Gazette. And that name was embossed and printed on different other enactments and documents. So, formally speaking, Bosnia-Herzegovina was present, whereas, from the point of view of substance, this situation was rather different. That is to say the substance of those Acts shows that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna does not stem from the constitutional and legal provisions in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but that it creates its own separate, legal system. This does not mean that in Herceg-Bosna the provisions were not at all applied of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It did not mean that. All it meant was that those provisions and laws were applied for which the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna had decided itself to implement. And I can quote if you deem necessary, several formulations from those provisions which testify to the fact that on the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna the laws of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina were in force only, unless otherwise prescribed. That is to say only unless they were not in keeping with the law and order establishment in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So that these provisions, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna demonstrated through these provisions its sovereign right to make decisions as to what laws would be applied on its own territory, and what laws and provisions were not applicable. Another example which shows the relationship towards the provisions of Bosnia-Herzegovina was a decision of the Constitutional Court of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which annulled all the most important enactments, including the act on the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna itself, because those enactments were in opposition to the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and its organs went on working just as if those provisions of the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Registrar has been provided with Z341.3, 341.4(a), 341.5(a) and 8(a) which were various decrees that were, in fact, enacted by Herceg-Bosna or which were borrowed -- selectively borrowed with qualifications from Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Constitutional Court decision of the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina to which Dr. Ribicic has referred is Z -- it's previously been admitted into evidence and it is Z216.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, are you aware if the only official invalidation of the pronouncements of Herceg-Bosna came from the Constitutional Court, or did the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina earlier react as well?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: The Constitutional Court adopted this decision only in September 1992, as far as I know, because it had problems in reaching the acts and enactments of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. But other organs, first of all, the Ministry for Legislation, and later on the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, adopted the position that the enactments passed in November 1991 were counter-constitutional; especially the justice ministry presented arguments for this view, as was done later on by the decision of the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Of course, the positions taken by the government and the ministry were not binding on the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, as did the Constitutional Court decision, which is binding for all bodies on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In that decision, the Constitutional Court states quite clearly that there is no constitutional groundwork for the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and that in forming that community, nobody can refer to intermunicipality cooperation, as was determined by the constitution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was in force at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, are you able to explain what you meant in your paper by "SAO-isation," and how did this affect the actions of Herceg-Bosna, "SAO-isation"? And what is "SAO"?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: SAO-isation is a concept which speaks of the formation of Serbian autonomous regions which came into being, which were formed in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina. What they were was activities on the part of the political party, the SDS, which established its own national regions, and it relied on the provisions of the constitution relating to intermunicipality cooperation for their establishment, and especially economic grounds for the establishment of these particular regions and communities. When it came to the formation of regions of this kind in the Republic of Croatia, the state organs of that republic reacted very quickly. The Constitutional Court and the Republic of Croatia annulled the formation, invalidated the formation, of regions of this kind, and I quote in my opinion a decision which relates to the SAO, S-A-O, of northern Dalmacija.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you comment -- I'm sorry. Continue.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbian Autonomous Regions began to be formed earlier on, before the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna came into being, and this was an expression of political organisation on the part of the Serbian people which was, at the same time, linked up with the so-called silent occupation of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the part -- or silent aggression of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the part of the Yugoslav People's Army, and all the forces it withdrew from Slovenia and Croatia were then concentrated into Bosnia-Herzegovina. That gave rise to a situation where politically and militarily speaking the Serbs were in control of two-thirds of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, with the idea of attaching this part of Bosnia-Herzegovina to what was termed Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, can you comment --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you comment, please, Dr. Ribicic, on the significance of the SAO-isation on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina with respect to the recognition of Bosnia's independence by Croats in the Republic of Croatia, as well as enunciated in the documents of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: The fact is that the SAO-isation of Bosnia-Herzegovina meant a silent or quiet aggression on Bosnia-Herzegovina and that this gave rise to a situation whereby a large portion of the territory, not only the portion inhabited by Serbs but the area which was also inhabited by the Muslims and Croats, was under that invisible occupation. That is the reason for which I write about this and my views, that for me, it was quite clear that one of the reasons for the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was precisely to set up a defence against this aggression. It is quite another matter in what way this could have been done effectively, how they could stand up to this aggression effectively in practice, and one possibility was to form the Croatian Communities; first of all of, Posavina and then in Herceg-Bosna and further afield. The second possible option was to tread a different path and not to follow the course started by the SDS party, but rather to unite all forces willing to defend the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was the subject of occupation and aggression, the kind that I mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I was asking additionally if the fact that what you've called the silent invasion, if you are considering it tantamount to the beginning of partition or attempted partition of Bosnia, what effect that had on the recognition by Herceg-Bosna, and the Croat community generally, of an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: When the SAO, Serbian Autonomous Regions, were formed in Croatia, there was a decisive reaction on the part of the authorities of the Republic of Croatia against this. When the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna appeared later on, what happened was that part of the official Croatian authorities supported that decision on the formation of Herceg-Bosna, and if we take into account the assessments made with regard to SAO-isation, then we can say that we were dealing with military criteria; that is to say, the Croatian authorities reacted in one way to the autonomous units that emerged in the Republic of Croatia, and the reactions to them were quite different to those, that is to say, which formed the autonomous communities which emerged in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The various preambles to the enactments mention the relationship -- address the relationship of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna to BiH, to Bosnia-Herzegovina. There are references to "so long as Bosnia remains unaffiliated with present or future Yugoslavia or remains independent or is not partitioned." Can you comment on the timing of the pronouncements, the enactments, relative to the already undertaken SAO-isation. In other words, was there already a partition in effect or an attempted partition?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: The attempt at partition began with the SAO-isations and not the formation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, but this attempt was boosted with the formation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna itself. If the representatives of the Croatian people had decided otherwise, it might not have come into being. As far as Bosnia-Herzegovina is concerned, an explanation of the decision to establish Herceg-Bosna emphasises the fact that it was a question of defending Croatian interests and Croatian territory but that the Croatian people were defending the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina, while others did not start partitioning it. There are differences there too between the original decision taken and the decision which was taken and published later on in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. In other words, until others started partitioning it, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes. The formulation is as follows, and I quote: "We strove for a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina, but we always emphasised that we would do so up to the point at which others begin to partition Bosnia-Herzegovina." If I were to quote Dr. Franjo Tudjman on that question, from the meeting I already mentioned on the 27th of December, held in Zagreb, then he too spoke about the fact that support to Bosnia-Herzegovina was necessary, first and foremost, because the Republic of Croatia was being jeopardised by the Republic of Serbia with the formation of the SAO-Krajina region, and he speaks about these efforts towards Bosnia-Herzegovina in the past. I can quote his position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must make some greater progress, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I try to bring this just to a point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, may I ask you, can you conclude, based on the timing that you have been discussing, that at the time of the formation of Herceg-Bosna, in effect, the partition which was a condition that would not allow recognition had already come about and therefore there was no intention to recognise an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina, that the condition of partition had begun; is that your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: The partition was never realised, but a decision was taken to divide Bosnia-Herzegovina, to partition it, and I'd like to emphasise that a decision of this kind was not made by the Sabor or assembly of the Republic of Croatia, or any other state organ, in the sense of an official decision on partitioning or attaching Herceg-Bosna to the Republic of Croatia. So that is a decision taken by a portion of the political leadership which was never officially voted in by the Croatian Sabor or assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Moving on to what has become known as the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, can you describe the changes which occurred within the structures of Herceg-Bosna when it reconstructed itself into the republic, which would have been 28 November 1993, taking into consideration what was happening in the International Community at that time.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: What happened there were five or six vital changes. The first change was in the fact that it was emphasised especially that Herceg-Bosna would remain within the composition of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; that is to say, there would no longer be an option for independence and for it to be part of the Republic of Croatia. The second difference lay in the fact that the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna now called itself a state community, which was not previously the case in the documents of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. The third difference lay in the fact that the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna no longer referred to the right of the Croatian people to self-determination but relied on the inalienable rights of the Croatian people as one of the constituent peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The fourth difference lay in the fact that special emphasis was laid on the fact that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna would realise its goals by peaceful means. The fifth difference referred to a respect and importance of international enactments on human rights and citizens rights. So the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, in much broader terms and much clearer terms than the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, emphasised the importance and application of the provisions on international human and citizens rights. Within that framework, later on, in a separate document which is titled "The Declaration on the Acceptance of Documents on the Protection and Realisation of Human Rights," and in certain other documents, "The Declaration on the House of Representatives," on the 8th of February, 1994, it emphasises the significance of this Tribunal as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, within --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: -- within the International Community, there was coming about something known as the Owen-Stoltenberg Agreement which contemplated a union of the three republics. Is that one of the factors that you had observed as being written into the legislation of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: I am not an expert in international law, but I was able to note that some things coincided; that is to say, the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, on the one hand, coincided with formulations that were made with the establishment of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. That is to say the union of the three republics is present in a similar formulation in this plan and in the documents relating to the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna itself. Furthermore, in literature, I found -- I came across views and opinions testifying to the fact that before this particular Owen-Stoltenberg Plan was elaborated, attempts were being made in practice on the ground to prepare the way for the realisation of this plan. So I can confirm, yes, that in my opinion the activities of the International Community were geared towards effecting a change in the attitude of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Registrar has received, for distribution, some of the laws which were referred to by Dr. Ribicic as Z1345.2(a), 1345.3(a), 1345.6(a), and then the actual -- 1345.7(a) and 1364 -- I'm sorry, 1464.6(a). They have been incorporated and referred to through a summary that Dr. Ribicic had. Dr. Ribicic, one quick question about the nature of the selective use of laws. During the existence of Herceg-Bosna's community, there appeared some aspect about the temporariness or in time of war only. Did this type of qualification or limitation tend to appear on the laws of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, or did you observe a more permanent character?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can notice certain differences, but I should like to stress that during the time of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, that particular formulation, that is to say that certain provisions relate to wartime and the imminent danger of war, that they had relative values. And if we look at the substance of those provisions, and the provisions enacted by the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, they were not of the kind that would relate only to questions which arose due to the danger and threat of war, but it was without any time limits and regulated many questions which did not have anything to do with war, or the threat of war. So that is what I know about the enactments of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Somers, I think that we should wind up our deliberations before the break, and that we should concentrate on aspects -- we are not dealing with constitutional theory, but focus on aspects which concern us, simple questions which concern this case; constitutional aspects, of course, having a bearing on our case. So please try and abbreviate without entering into the general realms of deliberations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I was going to ask the Court's advice. There are a few points simply on the changes of the governmental structure of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Would the Court want me to wait till after the lunch break? There are probably five or six questions now that are important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And anything else that you want to deal with, briefly, on the summary, Ms. Somers, you are free to do that. If you would like to look at it over the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was not in Court yesterday, and I was informed by Mr. Nice that the Defence has indicated they are accepting, essentially, the provisions of the summary. If Mr. Nice could elaborate on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I don't imagine they are accepting it. They are prepared to accept it as the evidence in chief, which is what I had suggested.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But any matters you want to elaborate, feel free to do so. But we'll try and move on to the cross-examination. I wonder if the Registrar would again raise the question of the heat in this room, which is already, despite not being the adjournment, which is still more than it should be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'll raise it with our department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And see if something can be done about it before we come back this afternoon. Or we shall go to Courtroom 2 again. Dr. Ribicic, could you come back, please, at half past 2, to get on with your evidence. Could you remember not to speak to anybody about it during the course of your evidence, and don't let anybody speak to you about it until it's over. Thank you very much. Half past 2 then. --- Luncheon recess taken at 10 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, as you indicated in your report, the presidency created the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, on 8 April 1992, as the supreme body responsible for the defence of the Croatian people in Herceg-Bosna, based on its powers that the presidency gave itself to appoint the executive and military bodies. Can you comment, please, briefly on the relationship of the presidency and the HVO particularly with respect to enactments or orders of the HVO, whether or not they were subordinate to and subject to veto by the presidency.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: The HVO of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was subordinated to the presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and this also holds true of municipal HVOs, that is, the HVOs formed in municipalities. The situation, however, radically changed when the HVO of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna became operational. The thing is that the HVO enjoyed a position which could be compared with the position of a government. So, as I said, it was subordinated to the presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, but in practice it discharged an executive function quite independently, and some of the acts adopted by the HVO could be said to contain some elements of legislative power. The question of supervision over the work of municipal HVOs was also regulated similarly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Then in response to my question about veto power by the presidency over enactments of the HVO, the presidency did -- or the HVO was accountable and subordinate to the presidency?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, quite, and the HVO of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna also had supervisory powers over municipal HVOs; that is, it could invalidate or abolish their acts and even disband municipal HVOs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Ms. Somers. I should like to ask Dr. Ribicic, in relation not to the right of veto but whether the presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna could issue instructions and orders to the HVO command; that is, positive instructions, because a veto is something negative, not to do something. I'm asking whether the presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna could issue instructions and orders to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: The HVO was accountable to the presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and could receive instructions for its work. So my answer is yes, the presidency could issue binding guidelines, binding instructions, to the HVO, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. In other words, the HVO was bound to comply with these instructions, with these guidelines.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Before I ask my next question, may I take the opportunity to mention that this entire report is Exhibit Z2811, and I wanted to make sure that gets on the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, under HR HB, the republic, did the presidency continue to exist as a concept?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: No. In the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the functions of the presidency were transferred to the House of Representatives of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. In a way, this is a discrepancy with other decisions and acts in effect in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna which lay an emphasis on the parliamentary organisation of that republic; that is, by transferring the functions from the presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna to the House of Representatives of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, thereby this -- no, sorry, not the House of Representatives, but House of Deputies, and thereby it was vested with somewhat stronger authority than a parliamentary body that other systems might have.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The supreme body of executive power, which has been called in your report the Vlada, that supreme power then becomes vested in a legislative body?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: I believe we can talk about the continuity between the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, meaning the functions of some bodies of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna were transferred to new bodies, to new agencies of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and this does not apply only to the transfer of powers to the Chamber of Deputies, but also from the HVO to the government, and the function of the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna to the president of the republic. Moreover, until the election of new bodies, these state functions were discharged by the bodies of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So this was a transitory solution pending the election of the new bodies and organs, so that the former bodies of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna discharged new functions, with new names, as bodies of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just to clarify some of those transitions from the community to the republic, your paper indicates that the HVO actually became the government or the Vlada, and that means that the HVO or the Vlada was now [Realtime transcript read in error "not"] accountable to the Chamber of Deputies or House of Representatives, which is another term we have used; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Just as, prior to that, the HVO was accountable to the presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You have suggested in your paper that the republic strengthened the position of the head of state, that is, the president of the republic. Can you comment, please, who was that president of the republic and indicate briefly how you see the position as strengthened.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Initially, as I have just said, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna did not have the position of head of state. Later on, it was discharged by the president of the presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, that is, as of July 1992 onward. But with the emergence of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the president of the republic acquired a new title; that is, he was no longer the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, he was now titled "President of the Republic," emphasising, therefore, his importance. And since the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna had proclaimed itself a state community, a state, we can now say, indeed, that the president of the republic had become the head of state of that particular state community, which can be likened to the head of state.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: My colleague asked me to point out to the stenographers that line 20 should indicate that "the HVO or Vlada is now accountable," instead of reading "not accountable."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Pursuant to that answer, Dr. Ribicic, I would ask you to take a look at a document which has been marked as Prosecution Exhibit Z1464.7, which I'd ask the Registrar please to take it as being shown for the first time. Sadly, we have only at this time the English translation, as well as the B/C/S. I hope to get a French one very soon. Dr. Ribicic, in December of '93, which is again addressed in your paper, the president of HR HB passed a decision establishing the presidential council. The document which you have in front of you, which is dated 17 February 1994, is a Narodni List, "Fundamental decision on the modification of the amendment of the fundamental decision on the creation and Proclamation of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna." Turning your attention to Article -- particular attention to Article 8(a), as well as generally the nature of the incremental powers given.
